findings.title: SELECT on order_items: full table scan, an index would help
findings.detail: Seq Scan on order_items reads the whole table (100 MB, never analyzed) to keep ~4.5k. An index on the filtered column(s) would find them directly. Tested `CREATE INDEX ON "order_items" ("order_id")`: estimated cost 26k → 13k (hypothetical index).

fix.text: An index lets the database find these rows without scanning the table. Add it with a migration and declare it on the model so `sync()` and new environments get it too.

findings.title: N+1: SELECT on order_items, once per row (up to 10× in a row)
findings.detail: Runs right after SELECT on orders (which returned up to 10 rows), once for each row. 1 loop in this capture, 10 executions, 660 ms in total.

fix.text: For each Order row, its OrderItem rows are fetched with their own query (`order.getOrderItems()` in a loop, or a lazy association). Load them together with the Order rows. `separate: true` fetches all children in one extra query (`WHERE "order_id" IN (…)`) instead of a JOIN that repeats every Order column per child.

findings.title: Large result from SELECT on products
findings.detail: Returns up to 5.0k rows with no LIMIT (215 kB per call on average). The application receives and builds an object for every row.

fix.text: The query loads every matching row and Sequelize builds a model instance for each. Paginate, select only the columns you use, and skip instances when you only read the data.
